transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Laura Chen, Diego Alvarez (Redwood); Maya Thompson, Ravi Singh, Emily Park (Summit Analytics)

Summary: quick Optimize walkthrough to align on batching and KV/prefix cache settings and to map to a cost model for their 100 qps conversational workload.

00:00 Laura Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Laura, AE on the account, and Diego is our solutions engineer. Quick agenda — we'll run through batching basics, prefix / K V cache options, cost model, and then map out a PoC.
00:17 Diego Alvarez: Hi, all. I'll start with a couple of slides then jump into a cost spreadsheet. Apologies if the slides are a little dense.
00:34 Maya Thompson: Thanks, Laura. Quick context — we're seeing about 100 qps peak, average session length around 120 tokens per turn, and target p95 latency under 250 ms. We're also sensitive to data residency and KMS encryption.
00:53 Diego Alvarez: Great, that helps. So first, batching — there are two approaches: micro-batching to hide GPU latency and continuous batching for throughput. For low latency SLOs you want tight per-request batching windows — say 5-10ms — but that reduces batching efficiency.
01:20 Emily Park: Can you quantify that — like how much cost delta are we talking if we move window from 5ms to 25ms?
01:31 Diego Alvarez: Roughly, with our cost model — and I'll send the sheet — at 100 qps and 120 tokens average, increasing batching window to 25ms can improve tokens-per-second by ~18-22%, which translates to about 12-18% cost savings on token compute, depending on model. That's with continuous batching and some prefix hit rate.
01:53 Ravi Singh: When you say prefix hit rate, is that the same as KV cache hit? We have several prompt prefixes that are common across many users.
02:05 Diego Alvarez: Yeah, prefix cache or KV cache — our system supports both. The important bit is hit distribution. If you get >40% prefix hits, the effective per-request cost drops dramatically because KV cache avoids re-computing early layers.
02:23 Maya Thompson: How do you size the KV/ prefix cache memory? We run into memory pressure on our current infra.
02:32 Diego Alvarez: Good q. Sizing depends on seq length, model size, and number of concurrent sessions. There's a rule of thumb: for 2K token KV cache per session and 1K concurrent sessions you'd need X GB — I'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet. Also, quantization and eviction policies matter; LRU for session-based workloads is typical.
02:56 Laura Chen: I'll drop the sizing doc link in the follow-up. We're also mindful of Dedicated vs Hosted — if Reserved Dedicated, you get predictable throughput and can tune cache sizing on the pool. Hosted works too but with less control over pinned memory.
03:18 Emily Park: Our security/compliance folks will want SOC2 and KMS details before Dedicated. Do you have that?
03:27 Laura Chen: Yes, we'll share SOC2 and our Private deployment KMS integration notes. Note Private has customer-managed KMS in the VPC.
03:36 Maya Thompson: Ok, good.
03:40 Diego Alvarez: Moving to the cost model — I'll screen-share the sheet now. (screen-share) The model takes inputs: qps, avg tokens per request, avg tokens output, batch window, cache hit rate, model type (float16 vs quantized), and whether you're on Dedicated or Hosted.
04:05 Diego Alvarez: Example: baseline with no KV cache, 5ms batch window, 100 qps, avg 120 tokens results in approximate 1.8M tokens/day and cost bracket A. If you enable a 45% cache hit rate and increase batch window to 20ms, tokens computed drops by ~40% leading to big savings.
04:35 Maya Thompson: Are you assuming a specific model? We rely on an instruction-tuned Llama variant right now.
04:44 Diego Alvarez: We used our curated open models as a proxy — for Llama-2-13B-ish behavior. Quantization (int8 / awq) reduces memory and improves throughput but may change quality. We always recommend validating on your eval set.
05:05 Ravi Singh: For the PoC, we want deterministic latency. How do you recommend we configure batching and cache to hit p95 < 250ms reliably?
05:17 Diego Alvarez: Recommendation: Dedicated pool with pre-warmed instances, batch window 8-12ms, KV cache with conservative TTL to keep active sessions warmed — that will generally meet p95. If you must stay Hosted, use smaller batch window and more aggressive auto-scale. We'll propose a config.
05:43 Speaker 1: (mumbling) about warm starts — does cold start affect KV hit?
05:48 Diego Alvarez: Yes, cold starts reduce cache hits and increase latency. For PoC we can provision a small Dedicated pool or use host with warm replica to avoid that.
06:01 Maya Thompson: Can we see a sample run with our traffic traces?
06:06 Laura Chen: Yes, that's an action item — Maya to share traces. Diego will run the sheet with those traces.
06:12 Diego Alvarez: I'll also model queue depth and tail latency. Remember that batching introduces a tradeoff between average throughput and tail latency.
06:28 Emily Park: Any notes on multi-tenant isolation? We have different business units.
06:33 Laura Chen: Dedicated supports isolated GPU pools per tenant; RBAC and VPC peering for network isolation. We'll include the architecture note in the follow-up.
06:46 Diego Alvarez: (shares link) Here's the benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood-internal.example.com/sheets/optimize-cost-model (placeholder link). I'll run an initial scenario now with 100 qps and a 45% prefix hit.
07:02 Diego Alvarez: Running numbers — with Llama-13B quantized and cache hits at 45%, effective compute tokens drop ~38% and GPU-hours drop ~35%, roughly correlating to 30-40% cost reduction vs baseline.
07:25 Maya Thompson: That seems promising. How sensitive is that to session length? If our sessions go to 400 tokens average?
07:33 Diego Alvarez: The longer the session, the more benefit from KV cache because repeated prefixes are amortized across tokens. With 400 tokens, relative savings increase. But memory demands for KV cache also rise.
07:50 Ravi Singh: Do you have metrics on eviction behavior under memory pressure? We can't afford high OOM events.
07:58 Diego Alvarez: Yes, we recommend configuring a memory soft-limit and LRU eviction; Redwood can surface cache eviction metrics in Console so you can tune. Diego: I'll include sample eviction dashboards in the follow-up.
08:15 Maya Thompson: How about network cost if we use Private / VPC peering?
08:22 Laura Chen: Network egress is customer-managed; we'll show typical numbers. Dedicated can be provisioned in customer region to reduce egress.
08:34 Emily Park: Any table that compares Hosted vs Dedicated on cost, latency, and control?
08:42 Diego Alvarez: Yes — in the spreadsheet: Hosted = lower up-front, less control; Dedicated = committed cost but much better predictability and tuning for batching/cache. I'll export the table.
08:55 Maya Thompson: For a PoC, we want to simulate our peak for 48 hours and measure p95. What's a realistic PoC scope?
09:04 Laura Chen: PoC scope — 2 weeks, run synthetic replay with your traces at 100 qps peak for 48-72 hours, include a Dedicated small pool or hosted warm replicas. We'll size and cost it in the estimate.
09:18 Ravi Singh: Is there a minimum committed spend for Dedicated?
09:22 Laura Chen: There is a reserved capacity commit for Dedicated — I'll include options in pricing: monthly or annual. More discount for annual.
09:30 Diego Alvarez: Also note fallback policies — if Dedicated pool is at capacity, Redwood routing can fall back to a compatible quantized variant in Hosted to maintain availability.
09:44 Maya Thompson: Ok, that helps. I also want to call out that we have encryption-at-rest reqs and our KMS is AWS KMS with external key management.
09:55 Laura Chen: Good to know — Private supports customer-managed KMS; for Hosted we have envelope encryption but we can discuss compliance options.
10:05 Emily Park: On evaluation, we want quality metrics — BLEU/ROUGE isn't useful here — we will provide prompt-based evals.
10:14 Diego Alvarez: Perfect — Redwood Optimize will track regression alerts tied to your eval prompts, and we can threshold quality vs latency.
10:23 Maya Thompson: Any competitors we should be aware of? We looked at OpenAI Endpoint and Anthropic — their hosted offering is simple but less config for caching. We're also considering self-hosted inference stacks.
10:36 Laura Chen: Right — that's common. In summary, Redwood gives more operational levers (batching, KV cache, quantization profiles) to tune cost vs latency.
10:48 Diego Alvarez: Quick demo: I'll flip through a Console view showing token-level cost and per-route tracing so you can see where tail latency comes from. (brief demo)
11:10 Diego Alvarez: Note console shows cache hit rate per model + per-route. You can set automatic fallback to a quantized variant if cost triggers a budget threshold.
11:25 Maya Thompson: That looks useful. A question from procurement — do you provide audit logs for all requests?
11:32 Laura Chen: Yes, audit logs and per-token billing are available for Dedicated and Private. We'll include sample log formats.
11:40 Emily Park: Great.
11:44 Laura Chen: Ok, to recap next steps: we'll send pricing, the benchmark/cost spreadsheet, example eviction and cache dashboards, SOC2/security docs, and then coordinate a PoC kickoff. Maya to share traces; Diego and I will produce a PoC plan.
12:02 Maya Thompson: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
12:06 Ravi Singh: Thanks, bye.
12:09 Laura Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up by EOD with links and the action items.

Notes on transcription quality: some mis-heard acronyms (K V cache transcribed as 'K V' sometimes) and speaker labels may be slightly off in places.
